claim: Organisms rely on inducible and constitutive immune defences to combat infection.
source: Organisms rely on inducible and constitutive immune defences to combat infection.
evidence: This is a general statement about immune systems that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Constitutive immunity enables a rapid response to infection but may carry a cost for uninfected individuals.
source: Constitutive immunity enables a rapid response to infection but may carry a cost for uninfected individuals
evidence: This statement reflects established theoretical understanding in immunology.

claim: Constitutive immunity is predicted to be favoured when infection rates are high.
source: leading to the prediction that it will be favoured when infection rates are high
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on evolutionary theory.

claim: Populations of Drosophila melanogaster evolved resistance when exposed to intense parasitism by the parasitoid wasp Leptopilina boulardi.
source: When we exposed populations of Drosophila melanogaster to intense parasitism by the parasitoid wasp Leptopilina boulardi, they evolved resistance by developing a more reactive cellular immune response.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental evolution study described in the manuscript.

claim: Resistant populations evolved resistance by developing a more reactive cellular immune response.
source: When we exposed populations of Drosophila melanogaster to intense parasitism by the parasitoid wasp Leptopilina boulardi, they evolved resistance by developing a more reactive cellular immune response.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental evolution study.

claim: Immune-inducible genes became constitutively upregulated in resistant larvae.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we found that immune-inducible genes had become constitutively upregulated.
evidence: This finding is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Resistant larvae differentiated precursors of specialized immune cells called lamellocytes that were previously only produced after infection.
source: This was the result of resistant larvae differentiating precursors of specialized immune cells called lamellocytes that were previously only produced after infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Populations evolved resistance by genetically hard-wiring the first steps of an induced immune response to become constitutive.
source: Therefore, populations evolved resistance by genetically hard-wiring the first steps of an induced immune response to become constitutive.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Uninfected individuals produce natural antibodies.
source: For example, uninfected individuals produce natural antibodies (Savage et al., 2017), immune cells, and antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Uninfected individuals produce immune cells and antimicrobial peptides.
source: For example, uninfected individuals produce natural antibodies (Savage et al., 2017), immune cells, and antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Induced immune responses are triggered after infection and frequently involve amplifying existing constitutive factors.
source: In contrast, induced immune responses are triggered after infection, which frequently involve amplifying existing constitutive factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about immune responses based on established knowledge.

claim: Induced immune responses can include immune cells proliferating and differentiating, and the massive upregulation of AMPs and cytotoxic molecules.
source: This can include immune cells proliferating and differentiating, and the massive upregulation of AMPs and cytotoxic molecules (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Immune defences can be costly, diverting limited resources from other fitness-related traits.
source: However, immune defences can be costly, diverting limited resources from other fitness-related traits (Bajgar et al., 2015) or damaging the host through immunopathology (Graham et al., 2005; Sadd and Siva-Jothy, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Immune defences can damage the host through immunopathology.
source: However, immune defences can be costly, diverting limited resources from other fitness-related traits (Bajgar et al., 2015) or damaging the host through immunopathology (Graham et al., 2005; Sadd and Siva-Jothy, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Costs of constitutive immunity are always present, even in the absence of infection.
source: While induced immune responses only incur these costs after infection, they are always present for constitutive immunity, even in the absence of infection.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of constitutive immunity.

claim: The trade-off between speed and cost is predicted to govern the allocation of host investment into constitutive and induced immunity.
source: This trade-off between speed and cost is predicted to govern the allocation of host investment into constitutive and induced immunity (Boots and Best, 2018; Shudo and Iwasa, 2001).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: Theoretical models predict that the frequency of host exposure to infection determines which type of defence should be favoured.
source: Theoretical models predict that the key parameter determining which type of defence should be favoured is the frequency that hosts are exposed to infection—more frequent exposure favours constitutive defences (Shudo and Iwasa, 2001).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by a citation.

claim: More frequent exposure to infection favours constitutive defences.
source: Theoretical models predict that the key parameter determining which type of defence should be favoured is the frequency that hosts are exposed to infection—more frequent exposure favours constitutive defences (Shudo and Iwasa, 2001).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by a citation.

claim: Bacteria tend to evolve phage resistance by altering surface receptors when exposure is high.
source: In support of this, bacteria tend to evolve phage resistance by altering surface receptors when exposure is high and rely on induced CRISPR-Cas immunity when exposure is low (Westra et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacteria rely on induced CRISPR-Cas immunity when phage exposure is low.
source: In support of this, bacteria tend to evolve phage resistance by altering surface receptors when exposure is high and rely on induced CRISPR-Cas immunity when exposure is low (Westra et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is variation in the extent of constitutive vs induced immunity within populations.
source: However, despite there being variation in the extent of constitutive vs induced immunity within populations (Jent et al., 2019), to our knowledge the key prediction that high rates of parasitism lead to induced immune responses becoming constitutively expressed has not been demonstrated.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The prediction that high rates of parasitism lead to induced immune responses becoming constitutively expressed has not been previously demonstrated.
source: However, despite there being variation in the extent of constitutive vs induced immunity within populations (Jent et al., 2019), to our knowledge the key prediction that high rates of parasitism lead to induced immune responses becoming constitutively expressed has not been demonstrated.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: In uninfected D. melanogaster larvae, there are two morphological and functional classes of hemocytes: plasmatocytes and crystal cells.
source: In uninfected larvae, there are two morphological and functional classes of hemocytes. Plasmatocytes constitute the majority of cells and have diverse functions including phagocytosis and AMP production (Honti et al., 2014). Crystal cells are a less abundant specialized cell type that produces the prophenoloxidase molecules PPO1 and PPO2, which are processed into enzymes required for the melanization of parasites and wound healing (Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plasmatocytes constitute the majority of hemocytes and have diverse functions including phagocytosis and AMP production.
source: Plasmatocytes constitute the majority of cells and have diverse functions including phagocytosis and AMP production (Honti et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Crystal cells are a less abundant specialized cell type that produces the prophenoloxidase molecules PPO1 and PPO2.
source: Crystal cells are a less abundant specialized cell type that produces the prophenoloxidase molecules PPO1 and PPO2, which are processed into enzymes required for the melanization of parasites and wound healing (Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PPO1 and PPO2 are processed into enzymes required for the melanization of parasites and wound healing.
source: Crystal cells are a less abundant specialized cell type that produces the prophenoloxidase molecules PPO1 and PPO2, which are processed into enzymes required for the melanization of parasites and wound healing (Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Infection can trigger an induced response where hemocyte cell types proliferate and lamellocytes differentiate.
source: Infection can trigger an induced response, where these cell types proliferate, and cells called lamellocytes differentiate from circulating plasmatocytes, and prohemocytes and plasmatocytes in the lymph gland (Cho et al., 2020; Honti et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lamellocytes differentiate from circulating plasmatocytes, and prohemocytes and plasmatocytes in the lymph gland.
source: Infection can trigger an induced response, where these cell types proliferate, and cells called lamellocytes differentiate from circulating plasmatocytes, and prohemocytes and plasmatocytes in the lymph gland (Cho et al., 2020; Honti et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lamellocytes are large flat cells with a specialised role in encapsulating and killing large parasites like parasitoids.
source: Lamellocytes are large flat cells with a specialised role in encapsulating and killing large parasites like parasitic wasps (parasitoids).
evidence: This is a description of lamellocyte function based on established knowledge.

claim: When a parasitoid lays its egg into D. melanogaster larvae, plasmatocytes adhere to the egg.
source: When a parasitoid lays its egg into D. melanogaster larvae, plasmatocytes adhere to the egg.
evidence: This describes the cellular immune response to parasitoid infection based on established knowledge.

claim: As lamellocytes differentiate they create additional cellular layers known as a 'capsule'.
source: Then, as lamellocytes differentiate they create additional cellular layers known as a 'capsule'.
evidence: This describes the cellular immune response to parasitoid infection based on established knowledge.

claim: The capsule is melanised by the activity of phenoloxidases produced in crystal cells and lamellocytes.
source: Finally, the capsule is melanised by the activity of phenoloxidases produced in crystal cells and lamellocytes (Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Melanin physically encases the parasitoid and toxic by-products of the melanisation reaction likely contribute to parasite killing.
source: The melanin physically encases the parasitoid and toxic by-products of the melanisation reaction likely contribute to parasite killing (Nappi et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is substantial genetic variation in susceptibility to parasitoid infection within D. melanogaster populations.
source: There is substantial genetic variation in susceptibility to parasitoid infection within D. melanogaster populations (Kraaijeveld and Godfray, 1999), and this is associated with an increase in the number of circulating hemocytes (Kraaijeveld et al., 2001; McGonigle et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Genetic variation in susceptibility to parasitoid infection is associated with an increase in the number of circulating hemocytes.
source: There is substantial genetic variation in susceptibility to parasitoid infection within D. melanogaster populations (Kraaijeveld and Godfray, 1999), and this is associated with an increase in the number of circulating hemocytes (Kraaijeveld et al., 2001; McGonigle et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: After 33 generations, a mean of 76% of flies survived infection in the high parasitism populations, compared to 10% in the no parasitism controls.
source: After 33 generations, a mean of 76% of flies survived infection in the high parasitism populations, compared to 10% in the no parasitism controls.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental evolution study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High parasitism populations increased in resistance over the generations.
source: In line with previous studies (Fellowes et al., 1998; McGonigle et al., 2017), the high parasitism populations increased in resistance over the generations (Figure 1B, Selection regime x Generation: χ2 = 91.41, d.f. = 1, p<10−15).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental evolution study with statistical support.

claim: Approximately half of larvae from selected populations encapsulate oil droplets.
source: In contrast, approximately half of larvae from selected populations encapsulate the oil droplet (Figure 1C; Selection Regime: χ2 = 73.35, d.f = 1, p=2×10−16).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the oil injection assay with statistical support.

claim: Populations that evolved without parasitism show a very limited reaction to oil droplets.
source: Populations that evolved without parasitism show a very limited reaction to the oil droplets (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the oil injection assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: High levels of parasitism led to the cellular immune system evolving a more active encapsulation response.
source: Therefore, high levels of parasitism led to the cellular immune system evolving a more active encapsulation response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the oil injection assay results.

claim: Forty-eight hours after flies were infected with parasitoid wasps there was a strong transcriptional response to infection.
source: Forty-eight hours after flies were infected with parasitoid wasps there was a strong transcriptional response to infection (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: When flies adapted to high parasitism conditions they showed similar transcriptional changes to infection, even when uninfected.
source: Strikingly, when flies adapted to high parasitism conditions they showed similar transcriptional changes, even when uninfected.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the bulk RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Taking the 173 genes that had at least a 50% change in transcript levels after infection or selection, in every case the direction of change was the same after infection and adaptation to high parasitism.
source: Taking the 173 genes that had at least a 50% change in transcript levels after infection or selection, in every case the direction of change was the same after infection and adaptation to high parasitism (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The 173 genes with at least a 50% change in transcript levels were enriched for biological roles such as cytoskeletal organization and cell adhesion.
source: These genes were enriched for biological roles such as cytoskeletal organization and cell adhesion (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: High rates of parasitism led to immune-induced genes atilla and PPO3 becoming constitutively upregulated.
source: Again, we found that high rates of parasitism led to these immune-induced genes becoming constitutively upregulated.
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR validation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transcriptional response to infection involved the same genes in the different populations.
source: We found that the transcriptional response to infection involved the same genes in the different populations (Figure 2B vs 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The magnitude of the changes in gene expression was substantially less in populations that had evolved under high parasite pressure.
source: However, the magnitude of the changes in gene expression was substantially less in populations that had evolved under high parasite pressure (Figure 2B vs 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The increase in constitutive gene expression has been matched by a decrease in induced expression.
source: Therefore, the increase in constitutive gene expression has been matched by a decrease in induced expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-seq data.

claim: Combining the constitutive and induced changes in gene expression, the hemocyte transcriptome after infection is similar in the populations that evolved under high levels of parasitism and the controls.
source: In support of this, combining the constitutive and induced changes in gene expression, the hemocyte transcriptome after infection is similar in the populations that evolved under high levels of parasitism and the controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 19,344 larval hemocytes were grouped into nine clusters based on their transcriptomes.
source: Excluding cells that did not express the pan-hemocyte markers Hemese or Serpent (Banerjee et al., 2019; Bernardoni et al., 1997), we grouped 19,344 larval hemocytes into nine clusters based on their transcriptomes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither infection nor selection leads to the appearance of new cell states.
source: Neither infection nor selection leads to the appearance of new cell states (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PLASM1 is classified as the cycling plasmatocyte state as it had the greatest number of replicating cells in the G2M or S phase.
source: The largest was PLASM1, which we classify as the cycling plasmatocyte state as it had the greatest number of replicating cells in the G2M or S phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a classification based on cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PLASM1 cluster contained 5712 cells with high expression of genes associated with plasmatocytes and actively replicating cells.
source: The 5712 cells in this cluster had high expression of genes associated with plasmatocytes (Col4a1, Pxn, eater, Hml, NimC1 Banerjee et al., 2019) and actively replicating cells (stg [Edgar and O'Farrell, 1990], polo [Glover, 2005] and scra Oegema et al., 2000; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a characterization of the PLASM1 cluster based on gene expression data.

claim: The PLASM2 cluster contained 2874 plasmatocytes that were enriched for genes encoding rRNA or involved in ribosome biogenesis.
source: The next largest cluster, PLASM2, contained 2874 plasmatocytes that were enriched for the genes encoding rRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) or involved in the ribosome biogenesis (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a characterization of the PLASM2 cluster based on gene expression data.

claim: The AMP cluster contained 196 cells with elevated expression of genes encoding antimicrobial and antifungal peptides.
source: The AMP cluster contained 196 cells with elevated expression of genes encoding antimicrobial and antifungal peptides, including Drs, Mtk and CecA1 (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a characterization of the AMP cluster based on gene expression data.

claim: The MET cluster contained 283 cells with high expression of heat shock proteins and genes involved in organic acid metabolism.
source: The MET cluster contained 283 cells with high expression of the heat shock proteins Hsp24 and Hsp27 and genes involved in organic acid metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a characterization of the MET cluster based on gene expression data.

claim: The crystal cells formed a single cluster of 906 cells.
source: The crystal cells formed a single cluster of 906 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the single-cell RNA-seq clustering shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Three clusters of cells (LAM 1, 2 and 3) had elevated expression of one or more lamellocyte marker genes and contained 1260, 5104, and 3000 cells, respectively.
source: Three clusters of cells, LAM 1, 2 and 3, had elevated expression of one or more lamellocyte marker genes (Banerjee et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and contained 1260, 5104, and 3000 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a characterization of the lamellocyte clusters based on gene expression data.

claim: All three scRNA-seq analyses identified very similar clusters of crystal cells, lamellocytes and AMP-expressing plasmatocytes.
source: We found that all three analyses identified very similar clusters of crystal cells, lamellocytes and AMP-expressing plasmatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the current study with two published scRNA-seq datasets.

claim: There was less correspondence between studies for the other clusters of plasmatocytes.
source: However, there was less correspondence between studies for the other clusters of plasmatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the current study with two published scRNA-seq datasets.

claim: In populations that evolved without exposure to parasitoids, infection resulted in a large increase in the number of cells in all three lamellocyte clusters.
source: In populations that evolved without exposure to parasitoids, infection resulted in a large increase in the number of cells in all three lamellocyte clusters (LAM1-3, Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In populations that evolved under high levels of parasitism, uninfected larvae had 3–5 fold more cells in LAM1 and 2.
source: In populations that evolved under high levels of parasitism, this inducible response becomes constitutive, with uninfected larvae having 3–5 fold more cells in LAM1 and 2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increase in constitutive lamellocyte precursors was matched by a reduction in the induced response, so the final number of cells in these clusters after infection was similar regardless of whether the populations had adapted to high or low parasitism rates.
source: However, this was matched by a reduction in the induced response, so the final number of cells in these clusters after infection was similar regardless of whether the populations had adapted to high or low parasitism rates (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: When populations evolved under high infection rates this led to the differentiation of specialised immune cells occurring in uninfected individuals.
source: Therefore, when populations evolved under high infection rates this led to the differentiation of specialised immune cells occurring in uninfected individuals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single-cell RNA-seq findings.

claim: A single lineage was found starting from the self-cycling plasmatocytes (PLASM1) and ending in LAM3.
source: By subclustering the cells and ordering them along a pseudotemporal scale, we found a single lineage starting from the self-cycling plasmatocytes (PLASM1) and ending in LAM3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Along the lamellocyte differentiation lineage there was a decrease in cell replication, with the largest fraction of cells in the G2M and S phase in PLASM1 and the largest fraction in G1 in LAM3.
source: Along this lineage there was a decrease in cell replication, with the largest fraction of cells in the G2M and S phase in PLASM1 and the largest fraction in G1 in LAM3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from cell cycle analysis along the differentiation trajectory.

claim: Controlling for the effects of cell cycle had a negligible impact on the clustering and the trajectory of lamellocyte differentiation.
source: Importantly, controlling for the effects of cell cycle had a negligible impact on the clustering (Supplementary file 4) and the trajectory of lamellocyte differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from cell cycle regression analysis.

claim: Genes involved in actin-filament based processes and biological adhesion were significantly upregulated in the terminal lamellocyte cluster.
source: Genes involved in actin-filament based processes and biological adhesion were significantly upregulated in the terminal lamellocyte cluster, possibly reflecting the changes in cell morphology and the role of lamellocytes in capsule formation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Genes involved in extracellular structure organization were down-regulated as cells differentiated into lamellocytes.
source: On the other hand, genes involved in extracellular structure organization were down-regulated as cells differentiated (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a result from gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LAM1 and LAM2 cells are immature lamellocytes, while LAM3 cells are mature lamellocytes.
source: Together, these results suggest that LAM1 and LAM2 cells are immature lamellocytes, while LAM3 cells are mature lamellocytes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trajectory analysis and gene expression patterns.

claim: The mature lamellocyte cluster LAM3 strongly corresponds to mature lamellocyte clusters defined in previously published larval hemocyte scRNA-seq data sets.
source: Consistent with this finding, the mature lamellocyte cluster LAM3 strongly corresponds to mature lamellocyte clusters defined in previously published larval hemocyte scRNA-seq data sets (Cattenoz et al., 2020 - LM-1; Tattikota et al., 2020 - LM2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the current study with published datasets.

claim: The immature lamellocyte clusters, LAM1 and 2, match the immature lamellocyte clusters in previously published studies.
source: Similarly, the immature lamellocyte clusters, LAM1 and 2, match the immature lamellocyte clusters in those studies (Cattenoz et al., 2020 - LM-2; Tattikota et al., 2020 - LM1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the current study with published datasets.

claim: The inducible production of immature lamellocytes (LAM1 and 2) has become entirely constitutive in the populations evolved under high rates of parasitism.
source: Comparing our populations, the inducible production of immature lamellocytes (LAM1 and 2) has become entirely constitutive in the populations evolved under high rates of parasitism, while the production of mature lamellocytes (LAM3) response remains largely inducible (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The production of mature lamellocytes (LAM3) remains largely inducible in populations evolved under high rates of parasitism.
source: Comparing our populations, the inducible production of immature lamellocytes (LAM1 and 2) has become entirely constitutive in the populations evolved under high rates of parasitism, while the production of mature lamellocytes (LAM3) response remains largely inducible (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 168 of the 173 genes with at least a 50% change in expression also change expression in the same direction as cells differentiate from plasmatocytes into lamellocytes.
source: The differentiation of these cells explains the changes in gene expression that we observed in pooled cells after infection or selection (Figure 1)—168 of the 173 genes with at least a 50% change in expression in Figure 1 also change expression in the same direction as cells differentiate from plasmatocytes into lamellocytes (PLASM1 vs LAM3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding linking the bulk RNA-seq and single-cell RNA-seq results.

claim: High infection rates result in the cellular immune response becoming 'primed' by constitutively producing the precursors of the cells required for parasite killing.
source: Together these results suggest that high infection rates result in the cellular immune response becoming 'primed' by constitutively producing the precursors of the cells required for parasite killing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings from the study.

claim: The proportion of morphologically identifiable lamellocytes increased after infection.
source: As expected, the proportion of morphologically identifiable lamellocytes increased after infection (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Treatment: χ2 = 48.14, d.f = 1, p=3.97×10−12).
evidence: This is a finding from morphological analysis with statistical support.

claim: There was little difference between selection regimes in the proportion of morphologically identifiable lamellocytes in either infected or uninfected larvae.
source: However, in contrast to our analysis of single-cell transcriptomes, there was little difference between selection regimes in the proportion of these cells in either infected or uninfected larvae (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Selection regime x Treatment: χ2 = 0.16, d.f = 1, p=0.69; Selection regime: χ2 = 0.41, d.f = 1, p=0.52).
evidence: This is a finding from morphological analysis with statistical support.

claim: While the transcriptional state of cells has been constitutively activated, the change in cell morphology, corresponding to the final step of lamellocytes maturation, remains an inducible response.
source: This suggests that while the transcriptional state of cells has been constitutively activated, the change in cell morphology, corresponding to the final step of lamellocytes maturation, remains an inducible response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological and transcriptional data.

claim: Both infection and adaptation to high parasitism rates increases the proportion of atilla positive cells.
source: In line with our scRNAseq data, both infection and adaptation to high parasitism rates increases the proportion of atilla positive cells (Figure 5C; Selection Regime x Treatment: F = 25.7, d.f = 1,8, p=0.0009).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry analysis with statistical support.

claim: Among atilla positive cells, infection had a large effect on cell size while selection had a small effect.
source: However, among the atilla positive cells, infection had a large effect on cell size (Figure 5C; Treatment: F = 41.6, d.f. = 1,7, p=0.0003), while selection had a small effect (Figure 5C; Selection Regime: F = 4.9, d.f. = 1,7, p=0.06).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry and cell size analysis with statistical support.

claim: Selection has resulted in the constitutive transcriptional activation of cells, while changes in lamellocyte morphology remain largely an inducible response.
source: Therefore, while selection has resulted in the constitutive transcriptional activation of cells, changes in lamellocyte morphology remain largely an inducible response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunohistochemistry and morphological data.

claim: Populations maintained under the high parasitism regime constitutively increased the number of hemocytes in circulation.
source: In addition to the change in the transcriptional state of cells in circulation, we found that the populations maintained under strong parasite pressure evolved a constitutive increase in the number of hemocytes in circulation (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Selection regime: χ2 = 22.37, d.f = 1, p=2.25×10−6).
evidence: This is a finding from hemocyte counting with statistical support.

claim: The number of crystal cells in the sessile compartment was not altered in populations maintained with high parasitism.
source: In accordance with this result, the number of crystal cells in the sessile compartment was not altered in populations maintained with high parasitism (Figure 5—figure supplement 6; Selection regime: χ2 = 0.014, d.f = 1, p=0.91).
evidence: This is a finding from crystal cell counting with statistical support.

claim: Populations that adapted to high rates of parasitism have a higher number of lymph glands containing immature lamellocytes.
source: However, populations that adapted to high rates of parasitism have a higher number of lymph glands containing immature lamellocytes (Figure 5D; main effect selection regime: χ2 = 6.90, d.f. = 1, p=0.009), and a non-significant trend towards a higher number of mature lamellocytes (Figure 5D; main effect selection regime: χ2 = 3.13, d.f. = 1, p=0.08).
evidence: This is a finding from lymph gland immunostaining with statistical support.

claim: In populations raised under high parasitism the proportion of disrupted lymph glands increased up to 60% at the late L3 larval stage.
source: Furthermore, in populations raised under high parasitism the proportion of disrupted lymph glands increased up to 60% at the late L3 larval stage (Figure 5E; selection regime*larval stage: χ2 = 3.46, d.f. = 1, p=0.06).
evidence: This is a finding from lymph gland disruption analysis with statistical support.

claim: Adaptation to high parasitism leads to an increase in both the differentiation of lamellocyte precursors in the lymph gland and the premature disruption of lymph glands.
source: Therefore, adaptation to high parasitism leads to an increase in both the differentiation of lamellocyte precursors in the lymph gland and the premature disruption of lymph glands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lymph gland analysis results.

claim: Infected larvae from populations selected under high parasitism produced more hemocytes overall and more lamellocytes specifically.
source: In line with our earlier results, infected larvae from populations selected under high parasitism produced more hemocytes overall and more lamellocytes specifically (total hemocytes, selection regime: χ2 = 70, d.f. = 1, p<2.2×10−16; lamellocytes, selection regime: χ2 = 14.92, d.f. = 1, p=0.11×10−3).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course hemocyte counting with statistical support.

claim: The dynamics of lamellocyte production differs between selection regimes, with populations selected under high parasitism producing higher proportions of lamellocytes at earlier time points.
source: Supporting our hypothesis, the dynamics of lamellocyte production differs between selection regimes, with populations selected under high parasitism producing higher proportions of lamellocytes at earlier time points (Figure 5—figure supplement 4; Lamellocyte proportion, selection regime*time point: χ2 = 36.56, d.f. = 3, p=5.69×10−8).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course hemocyte counting with statistical support.

claim: At 12 hr post infection, lamellocyte concentration was eight times higher in the populations that had evolved under high parasitism rates while total hemocytes was 2.5 times higher.
source: At the early timepoint of 12 hr post infection, lamellocyte concentration was eight times higher in the populations that had evolved under high parasitism rates while total hemocytes was 2.5 times higher (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from time-course hemocyte counting.

claim: Constitutive activation of immune defences allows hosts to mount more rapid immune responses.
source: Altogether, these results support the hypothesis that constitutive activation of immune defences allows hosts to mount more rapid immune responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-course hemocyte data.

claim: Natural selection favours constitutive defences when infection is common.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that natural selection favours constitutive defences when infection is common (Boots and Best, 2018; Shudo and Iwasa, 2001; Westra et al., 2015) by demonstrating that an inducible immune response becomes constitutive when populations frequently encounter a parasite.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the experimental data and citations to theoretical work.

claim: An inducible immune response becomes constitutive when populations frequently encounter a parasite.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that natural selection favours constitutive defences when infection is common (Boots and Best, 2018; Shudo and Iwasa, 2001; Westra et al., 2015) by demonstrating that an inducible immune response becomes constitutive when populations frequently encounter a parasite.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental evolution study.

claim: Drosophila populations evolve to produce immature lamellocytes constitutively if they are frequently exposed to infection.
source: Our results show that Drosophila populations evolve to produce these cells constitutively if they are frequently exposed to infection.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental evolution study.

claim: Populations evolved with high levels of parasitism by Asobara tabida showed no significant overlap of differentially expressed genes between selection and infection.
source: Our results contrast with populations evolved with high levels of parasitism by the parasitoid wasp Asobara tabida, where there was no significant overlap of differentially expressed genes between selection and infection (Wertheim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: The difference between studies could result from the different genetic basis of resistance to the two wasp species.
source: The difference between the studies could also result from the different genetic basis of resistance to the two wasp species (Poirie et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies supported by a citation.

claim: Populations that adapt to high parasitism rates have their cellular immune defences in a state of readiness, with the final step of massive lamellocyte differentiation remaining an inducible response.
source: The change in the transcriptional state of constitutive cells was not accompanied by morphological differentiation, suggesting that populations that adapt to high parasitism rates have their cellular immune defences in a state of readiness, with the final step of massive lamellocyte differentiation remaining an inducible response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined transcriptional and morphological data.

claim: Genes involved in cytoskeleton dynamics such as βTub60D and shot are among the genes with the greatest increases in expression as lamellocytes differentiate.
source: Genes involved in cytoskeleton dynamics such as βTub60D and shot are among the genes with the greatest increases in expression as lamellocytes differentiate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 5) and these may be required for the final step of changing cell shape (Rizki and Rizki, 1994).
evidence: This is a finding from the trajectory analysis with a citation supporting the functional interpretation.

claim: Populations from both selection regimes had very similar hemocyte compositions in the late stages of the immune response.
source: Furthermore, the late stages of the immune response were not qualitatively altered after selection. Populations from both selection regimes had very similar hemocyte compositions in the late stages of the response, which is similar to patterns reported from populations artificially selected with Asobara tabida (Salazar-Jaramillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with a citation to a similar observation in another study.

claim: Trehalase and the trehalose transporter Tret1-1 are upregulated in hemocytes after parasitoid infection.
source: In support of previous results, we found that Trehalase and the trehalose transporter Tret1-1 are upregulated in hemocytes after parasitoid infection (Figure 2; Bajgar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNA-seq data that confirms previous research.

claim: These metabolic genes are also upregulated in uninfected larvae after adaptation to high parasitism pressure.
source: We found that these genes are also upregulated in uninfected larvae after adaptation to high parasitism pressure (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The metabolic cost of immunity may be borne by uninfected flies in resistant populations, potentially contributing to the cost of evolving resistance.
source: This suggests that the metabolic cost of immunity may be borne by uninfected flies in our resistant populations, potentially contributing to the cost of evolving resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the metabolic gene expression data.

claim: Whether the host or parasitoid survives is a race between parasitoid development and the formation of a cellular capsule by the immune system.
source: After infection, whether the host or parasitoid survives is a race between parasitoid development and the formation of a cellular capsule by the immune system (Kim-Jo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Parasitoid wasps inject venom proteins and virus like particles during oviposition to suppress the host immune system.
source: To increase their success, parasitoid wasps inject venom proteins and virus like particles (VLPs) during oviposition to suppress the host immune system (Labrosse et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The L. boulardi strain used in this study affects lamellocyte differentiation.
source: These factors affect different components of the immune system (Poirié et al., 2014), with the L. boulardi strain used in this study affecting lamellocyte differentiation (Leitão et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Constitutive activation of cellular immunity may be a way to circumvent the suppressive effects of wasp venoms and VLPs by killing the parasite before immunity is suppressed.
source: Thus, resistant populations must circumvent the suppressive effects of the wasp venoms and VLPs, and constitutive activation of cellular immunity may be a way to achieve this by killing the parasite before immunity is suppressed.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how constitutive immunity provides resistance.

claim: Populations adapted to high levels of parasitism evolved two phenotypes that likely explain their higher resistance: producing more hemocytes in homeostasis and producing lamellocytes more rapidly upon infection.
source: We find that populations adapted to high levels of parasitism evolved two phenotypes that likely explain their higher resistance. Firstly, they produce more hemocytes in homeostasis, which leads to a faster increase in circulating hemocytes in early time points of infection. Secondly, they produce lamellocytes more rapidly upon infection, likely largely due to the constitutive production of immature lamellocytes.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: There is an increase in the constitutive expression of PPO3 in populations adapted to high rates of parasitism.
source: Furthermore, cytotoxic molecules could be more readily available as there is an increase in the constitutive expression of PPO3 in populations adapted to high rates of parasitism.
evidence: This is a finding from the RNA-seq data.

claim: PPO3 encodes an intracellular prophenoloxidase produced by lamellocytes that, when activated, is responsible for the capsule melanization.
source: PPO3 encodes an intracellular prophenoloxidase produced by lamellocytes that, when activated, is responsible for the capsule melanization (Dudzic et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The constitutive activation of the cellular immune response likely explains the greatly increased resistance of populations adapted to high rates of parasitism.
source: We conclude that the constitutive activation of the cellular immune response likely explains the greatly increased resistance of populations adapted to high rates of parasitism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.
